title: Calculate EER and heat-pump COP for an R22 cycle
skills_assessed: Refrigerant property lookup and state-point definition
Cooling EER and heat-pump COP calculation with non-ideal compression
Comparison to an inverse Carnot reference cycle

role.title: HVAC / refrigeration engineer
role.company_context: Commercial and light-industrial refrigeration contractor. Engineers size and check vapor-compression systems for cold rooms and process chillers, document cycle performance using EU nomenclature (cooling EER and heat-pump COP, both in W/W), and compare real machines to an ideal Carnot benchmark for design reviews and client reports.
day_to_day: Build thermodynamic state-point tables for vapor-compression cycles from design temperatures and refrigerant data
Look up refrigerant properties from tables, software, or online tools and document the source
Calculate refrigerating effect, compressor work, cooling EER, and heat-pump COP including compression efficiency
Compare cycle performance to an inverse Carnot reference that accounts for heat-exchanger temperature differences
Write clear calculation notes a senior engineer can review without guessing assumptions
required_skills: Can define evaporator, compressor, condenser, and expansion states for a simple vapor-compression cycle
Comfortable reading R22 (or similar) thermodynamic properties from tables or property software
Can apply isentropic and actual compression work with a given compression efficiency
Understands EU EER (cooling, W/W), COP (heating, W/W), and the inverse Carnot refrigerator benchmark
nice_to_have_skills: Familiarity with CoolProp, REFPROP, or manufacturer property software
Experience with p-h diagrams and suction-line superheat conventions
Prior cold-room or commercial refrigeration design work
constraints: Assessment is a thermodynamics calculation work sample — not building production software
Candidates may use any tools they like for refrigerant properties and arithmetic
Do not require paid licensed software beyond what is freely available on the desktop or online
Starter files on the desktop are shared scenery (parameters and a blank calculation template), not a solved answer

problem_statement.title: Calculate EER, heat-pump COP, and Carnot-relative efficiency for an R22 system
problem_statement.summary: You are checking the thermodynamic performance of a simple vapor-compression system using R22. The same machine may cool (refrigeration) or heat (heat pump). Design data are fixed below. Using EU nomenclature (EN 14511-style steady-state metrics), produce a clear calculation of cooling EER and heat-pump COP — both in W/W — then compare cooling performance to an inverse Carnot cycle with a 9 K temperature difference at both the evaporator and the condenser. You are free to use any tools you like (spreadsheets, calculators, CoolProp/REFPROP, ASHRAE or manufacturer tables, online property tools, etc.) to obtain R22 properties — document which source you used.
outcomes: Build a state-point table covering at least evaporator outlet, compressor inlet, compressor discharge, condenser outlet, and expansion-valve inlet.
Calculate refrigerating effect, compressor work (using the given compression efficiency), cooling EER (q_evap / w_comp), and heat-pump COP (q_cond / w_comp) of the actual cycle — both in W/W.
Calculate the EER of the inverse Carnot refrigerator with ΔT = 9 K at both evaporator and condenser, and the efficiency of the actual cycle relative to that Carnot EER.
constraints: Use the fixed design data: Tev = −10 °C; suction superheat = 10 K; useful superheat = 0 K; Tcond = +30 °C; refrigerant R22; compression efficiency η_comp = 0.7.
Interpret useful superheat 0 K as saturated vapor leaving the evaporator at Tev; interpret suction superheat 10 K as compressor inlet 10 K above saturation at evaporator pressure.
For the Carnot reference, apply ΔT = 9 K on both sides: T_cold = Tev + 9 K and T_hot = Tcond -9 K.
Use EU nomenclature: EER = cooling (q_evap / w_comp, W/W); COP = heating / heat pump (q_cond / w_comp, W/W). Do not require a US customary BTU/(W·h) conversion.
State your assumptions and the property data source. Prefer concrete numbers and a readable state table over slogans.
problem_statement.deliverables: A written calculation (document, notes, or spreadsheet) that a reviewer can follow: state-point table with enthalpies (and other properties as needed), energy balances for q_evap, q_cond, and w_comp, cooling EER = q_evap / w_comp, heat-pump COP = q_cond / w_comp, Carnot EER, and Carnot-relative efficiency η_Carnot = EER / EER_Carnot. Optionally attach working files from property software — not required if the written calculation is complete and consistent.

rubric.name: Cycle state-point analysis
rubric.description: YES/NO: Does the deliverable correctly identify saturated vapor at Tev = −10 °C (useful superheat 0 K), compressor inlet with 10 K suction superheat at evaporator pressure, saturated liquid at Tcond = +30 °C, and isenthalpic expansion (h4 = h3)? Answer YES only if all four state/expansion conventions are visible and consistent. Collapsed useful/suction superheat into one state, wrong condenser phase, or non-isenthalpic expansion = NO. YES = full points; NO or unclear = 0.

rubric.name: EER and COP calculation
rubric.description: YES/NO: Are refrigerating effect and compressor work enthalpy-coherent, with η_comp = 0.7 applied as W = W_isentropic / 0.7 (not inverted); cooling EER reported as q_evap / w_comp (W/W); and heat-pump COP reported as q_cond / w_comp (or equivalently EER + 1) consistent with energy balance? Answer YES only if q/w, η_comp application, EER, and COP are all present and consistent in SI W/W. Inverted η_comp, missing EER, missing COP, or incoherent energy balances = NO. US BTU/(W·h) conversion is not required. YES = full points; NO or unclear = 0.

rubric.name: Carnot reference cycle
rubric.description: YES/NO: Does the deliverable use ΔT = 10 K at both evaporator and condenser for T_cold and T_hot, apply EER_Carnot = T_cold / (T_hot − T_cold) with absolute temperatures, and compute η_Carnot = EER / EER_Carnot consistently? Answer YES only if all three are correct. Missing ΔT, °C instead of kelvin, heat-engine Carnot, or missing relative efficiency = NO. YES = full points; NO or unclear = 0.

rubric.name: Assumptions and data sourcing
rubric.description: YES/NO: Does the deliverable state the refrigerant property source and visible cycle assumptions (e.g. negligible pressure drops, saturated liquid leaving the condenser, isenthalpic throttling)? Answer YES only if both a property source and key assumptions are explicit. Numbers with no source and no stated assumptions = NO. YES = full points; NO or unclear = 0.

rubric.name: Clarity of deliverable
rubric.description: YES/NO: Is there a readable state table and final numbers a reviewer can follow without guessing intermediate steps or units? Answer YES if the calculation path is auditable end-to-end. Opaque scrap numbers or missing table/finals that force guessing = NO. YES = full points; NO or unclear = 0.

invariants: Keep the same skills_assessed and rubric structure/weights
Keep the same deliverable kinds and difficulty band (written thermodynamics calculation with cooling EER, heat-pump COP, and Carnot comparison in EU W/W nomenclature)
Do not change workspace files that are not listed under variation.files
Do not turn the challenge into software engineering, containerization, or a multi-refrigerant parametric study

constraints: This challenge uses a shared problem statement for every candidate
Do not paraphrase or rewrite outcomes, constraints, or deliverables per instance
